1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6.name: Chigorin Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6.background: Named after the 19th-century Russian master Mikhail Chigorin. Vasily Smyslov used it against Garry Kasparov in the 1980s and drew, and Alexander Morozevich, who is perhaps the only modern grandmaster to play it regularly, published a book on it with Vladimir Barskij in 2007.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: The most ambitious reply: the knight joins the c4 pawn in attacking d5, which only the queen defends, so Black must settle the tension in the centre at once. White keeps the space advantage and the initiative, and Black has to find active piece play to compensate.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Chigorin Defence

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.cxd5.strategy: Releases the tension and forces the issue: the pawn on d5 attacks the knight on c6, so Black recaptures with the queen at once. Black gets quick development and piece pressure against d4 in return for the early queen sortie, and White has to meet it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends d4 against the knight on c6 and develops, but spends the move on defence instead of increasing the pressure on d5. A sound, calm choice that keeps White's centre intact, though Black can build up active play while White is still catching up in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: The natural recapture: the queen takes the pawn that was attacking the c6 knight and stands in the centre at once, where it adds to the pressure on d4. Black has no central pawn left, so the plan is quick development, with the queen exposed to a tempo-gaining knight move.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and attacks d4 a second time, so White has to react at once. Black gives up the central pawn on d5 and relies on piece pressure against White's centre, trying to hold the extra pawn only as long as it serves that plan.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 in the classical way, but the knight on c6 is badly placed for it: it blocks the c-pawn, which normally supports d5 or strikes at White's centre. A solid but passive set-up in which Black has misplaced a piece.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: A gambit that offers the e-pawn at once to open lines for the pieces and hit d4. White does best not to take it but to strike at the c6 knight, which has to lose time moving. Black gets activity at the cost of tempi and central control.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Chigorin Defence, Tartakower Gambit

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, with an attack on the knight that guards d4 and e5. Together with the knight on c6 it keeps the pressure on d4, so White has to decide at once how to meet it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e5.strategy: A gambit that offers the e-pawn at once to open the position for the pieces and attack d4. White can accept and keep the pawn, so Black must show that the lead in development and open lines are worth a pawn. A risky practical try.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Chigorin Defence, Lazard Gambit
